group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 37-year-old man presented to the emergency department this afternoon after experiencing three days of worsening fatigue, exertional shortness of breath, and a new cough productive of green-yellow sputum that began the previous night. He drove himself from home, pausing only to gather a list of medications supplied by his dialysis center; he deliberately avoided taking any over-the-counter antipyretics or inhalers and did not receive supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, or nebulized therapy en route so that hospital staff could evaluate his unmodified physiology. The patient was diagnosed eight years ago with non-ischemic systolic dysfunction attributed to viral myocarditis, with a most recent echocardiogram three months prior demonstrating an ejection fraction near 30 % and mild biatrial enlargement; carvedilol 25 mg twice daily and low-dose torsemide are part of his usual regimen. Five years ago he developed progressive glomerulosclerosis complicated by uremia, requiring thrice-weekly hemodialysis—his last session ended the evening before presentation; the nephrologist’s notes document persistent metabolic acidosis between treatments and intermittent symptomatic hyponatremia, but he has never started peritoneal dialysis or been evaluated for transplant. He denies any prior cerebrovascular accidents, seizures, chronic liver disorders, or malignant disease, and his vaccination record confirms receipt of pneumococcal conjugate and annual influenza injections. He works remotely as a software engineer, lives with his partner in a second-floor apartment, climbs a flight of stairs daily without baseline limitation, and has never smoked; alcohol intake is limited to an occasional glass of wine, and he abstains from illicit drugs. Upon arrival he sat upright on the stretcher, conversing in full sentences without confusion and accurately stating the date, location, and reason for visit. Skin was warm and dry with no peripheral edema beyond trace pitting at the ankles—unchanged from his cardiology baseline. Untreated triage vitals were as follows: oral temperature 99.2 °F, regular pulse 80 beats min⁻¹, automated blood pressure 152/86 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 11 breaths min⁻¹ with tidal volumes judged adequate, and pulse oximetry 97 % on ambient air at sea-level altitude. Neck veins were estimated at 5 cm above the sternal angle while he sat at 45°, similar to previous examinations. Cardiac auscultation revealed a normal S1 and S2 with a soft third heart sound but no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Lung examination disclosed markedly reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right lower posterior hemithorax with faint egophony just superior to that zone; vesicular breath sounds were preserved elsewhere without wheezes or crackles. The abdomen was soft and non-tender with a palpable left forearm arteriovenous fistula bruiting briskly; no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites was appreciated. Neurologic screening showed equal and reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, symmetric facial expression, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. Bedside glucometer read 116 mg dL⁻¹ immediately before phlebotomy. Venous chemistries obtained within ten minutes—prior to any saline flushes except those required to maintain catheter patency—revealed profound hyponatremia at 110 mEq L⁻¹, potassium 4.8 mEq L⁻¹, chloride 92 mEq L⁻¹, bicarbonate 14 mEq L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 54 mg dL⁻¹, and serum creatinine 7.0 mg dL⁻¹, all representing typical inter-dialytic values for him except for the lower than usual sodium. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 13.9 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ with 88 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 21 %, hemoglobin 7.1 g dL⁻¹, and platelets 265 × 10⁹ L⁻¹. An arterial sample drawn from the left radial artery while he continued to breathe room air demonstrated pH 7.14, PaCO₂ 30 mm Hg, PaO₂ 104 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 11 mEq L⁻¹, confirming a severe metabolic acidosis with only partial respiratory compensation and no hypoxemia. Serum lactate measured 2.0 mmol L⁻¹. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any medications or fluids displayed a homogeneous opacity obscuring the right costophrenic angle with a classic meniscus sign and associated basilar consolidation, while the cardiac silhouette appeared mildly enlarged but unchanged from a film six months earlier. Electrocardiography showed sinus rhythm at 82 beats min⁻¹ with low-voltage QRS complexes and nonspecific ST-T changes identical to prior tracings. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigen assays for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a respiratory viral panel were dispatched prior to antibiotic administration. As of this documentation he remains seated comfortably on the gurney breathing ambient air, has not yet received antimicrobials, intravenous crystalloids, diuretics, vasopressors, antipyretics, bronchodilators, or dialysis, and therefore every physiologic observation, imaging finding, and laboratory value cited above reflects his presentation before any hospital intervention.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: a man receives his age in points (37); no nursing-home residence (0). Subtotal = 37.
- Comorbidities: systolic heart failure (EF about 30%) = 10; dialysis-dependent renal disease = 10. No malignancy, liver disease, or cerebrovascular disease = 0. Subtotal = 20.
- Examination: alert; RR 11 (<30/min), systolic BP 152 (not <90 mm Hg), temperature 99.2 °F (neither <35 nor ≥40 °C), and pulse 80 (<125/min). Subtotal = 0.
- Laboratory findings: arterial pH 7.14 (<7.35) = 30; BUN 54 (≥30 mg/dL) = 20; sodium 110 (<130 mEq/L) = 20; hematocrit 21% (<30%) = 10. Glucose 116 (<250 mg/dL) and room-air PaO2 104 (not <60 mm Hg) each score 0. Subtotal = 80.
- Radiograph: the meniscus obscuring the right costophrenic angle indicates a pleural effusion = 10.
Total = 37 + 20 + 0 + 80 + 10 = 147.
Final answer: 147
